fetched_contents.text: Lignocellulose dissociation with biological pretreatment towards the biochemical platform: A review 1. Introduction According to reports, fossil fuels and other nonrenewable resources are in short supply. In this context, the utilization of renewable energy and its derivatives as substitutes can effectively reduce the dependence on nonrenewable energy, thereby achieving sustainable development and economic benefits [1]. Lignocellulose is an abundant renewable biomass resource on earth, with an annual output of more than 20 billion tons [2], including wood, plants, agricultural waste, forest residues and municipal solid waste, which can be converted into eco-friendly high value-added products [3]. It was reported that if all straw waste in China could be converted into hydrogen, the energy generated would be equivalent to a total of 170 million tons of standard coal [4]. Moreover, the production of biofuels from lignocellulose could alleviate the pressure caused by rapid energy consumption. Biofuel conversion technologies, such as those producing bioethanol, biohydrogen and biomethane, are mature. Moreover, high-value chemicals produced from lignocellulose increase the profitability. However, the large-scale utilization of lignocellulose is still challenging. Enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose and hemicellulose is a key step in the transformation process, but the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose hinders the process by inhibiting enzymatic interactions (Fig. 1) [5], and the unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin also inhibits the enzymatic hydrolysis process [6]. In recent years, pretreatment has emerged as an effective approach to overcome these bottlenecks, thereby eliminating the compact and complex structure of biomass components and improving the accessibility of enzymes to cellulose. Pretreatment can accelerate the dissociation of fibers, promote biomass conversion, and hydrolyze polysaccharides into monosaccharides. Pretreatment also decreases the lignin contents, cellulose crystallinity and energy consumption [7]. In the lignocellulose process, effective pretreatment should meet the following requirements: (1) conducive to subsequent hydrolysis; (2) avoid producing by-products that inhibit enzyme saccharification; (3) be economically feasible; and (4) reduce pollution and waste of resources. At present, physical, chemical and biological treatments have been widely used for lignocellulose pretreatment. Physical treatments include mechanical crushing, ultrasonic treatment, microwave treatment, but these consume a lot of energy and are usually used as an auxiliary method. Chemical treatments have the advantage of high efficiency. For instance, rice straw treated with KOH and urea could obtain 92.38% sugar yield after 32.47% of lignin was removed under the optimal conditions [8]. However, the traditional chemical reagents have some disadvantages, such as the incomplete recovery of polysaccharides, possible generation of inhibitors and the risk of environmental pollution, thereby affecting the production efficiency [9]. Recently, ionic liquids have been used in pretreatment due to their non-flammable, non-volatile and recyclable characteristics [10]. When rice straw was treated with 1-H-3-methylmorpholinium chloride ionic liquid with water as co-solvent for 5 h, the ethanol production yield increased from 21.9% to 64% [11]. However, the high cost of ionic liquids limits large-scale implementation. Therefore, other types of green solvents have been developed as good substitutes for traditional reagents. It was reported that a high lignin removal rate of 73.17% was obtained after pretreatment with 10% ethylenediamine (EDA) and 200 °C. Compared with traditional alkali treatment, the residual EDA in wastewater can be separated by simple evaporation [12]. In addition, deep eutectic solvent (DES) has been shown to be a highly cost-effective and promising solvent [13]. Despite the fact that the lignin removal rate of DES might not be as high as that of alkali reagents, lignin pretreated with DES was substantially depolymerized and no condensation structure was observed [14]. The lignin from the corn stover was effectively removed after pretreatment with DES consisting of quaternary ammonium salts and hydrogen donors. After hydrolysis, no unfavorable inhibitors to the subsequent fermentation process were produced, indicating that DES possesses good biocompatibility [15]. In addition, it was found that the energy required for DES pretreatment was 28% and 72% lower than that of NaOH pretreatment and the steam explosion process, respectively [16]. These results all reflect the potential value of DES. Nevertheless, there are still challenges in the application of DES, whose inherent properties such as high viscosity and hygroscopicity may limit its application in biomass pretreatment. At the same time, further research is needed to identify ways in which to efficiently recover DES [10]. In short, traditional physical and chemical pretreatments require special equipment, and inhibitors can be produced in the process, which is inconducive to subsequent fermentation. Due to the great influence of pretreatment on downstream technologies, from the overall economic perspective, the eco-friendly characteristics make biological pretreatment stand out. Relatively speaking, biological methods consume less energy and do not produce inhibitors during the treatment process because it is carried out under mild conditions. There are a large number of microorganisms in nature that can be applied in biological pretreatment. The degradation capability of microorganisms mainly originates from their unique enzymatic systems. Lignolytic enzymes such as lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase and laccase have been applied to open the recalcitrant structure of lignocellulose. fetched_contents.text: Ligninolytic enzymes and its mechanisms for degradation of lignocellulosic waste in environment 1. Introduction Lignocellulosic waste is considered as a chief component of renewable biomass on the Earth (Saini et al., 2015). This consists of three major components such as cellulose (40%–50%), hemicelluloses (25%–30%) and lignin (15%–20%) (Chaurasia, 2019). Cellulose is the primary polysaccharide as constituent of lignocellulosic materials that consist of hundred to over ten thousands β-1, 4 linked D-glucose units in unbranched linear chains. This is known as microfibrils with 3–5nm wide and many micrometers in length (Horn et al., 2012). Each cellulose chain-linked side by side through hydrogen bonding and van der waals interactions into microfibrils arrangement which are reported to consist 24 to 36 chains based on x-ray scattering data and the information available regarding the cellulose synthesis (Anwesha et al., 2011; Horn et al., 2012). Each cellulose microfibrils is synthesized from the spontaneous bundling and crystallization with dozens of the linked β-D glucan chains, each of which is made by a cellulose synthase (CESA) protein (Cosgrove, 2005). While hemicellulose is arranged in forms of strips tightly linked with cellulose and lignin in plant cell walls, it contains branched polysaccharide mainly xylans and mannans. It contains branched heterogenous polysaccharides of pentose (xylose and arabinose), hexoses (glucose, mannose, and galactose) and sugar acids (e.g. acetic, galacturonic and glucuronic) (Dimarogona et al., 2012). There is the presence of five monomeric sugars namely D-glucose, D-mannose, D-galactose, D-xylose and L-arabinose linked by β-1, 4-glycosidic bonds, that consist of both liners and branched heteropolymers. The major hemicelluloses in hardwoods are xylans (15%–30% dry weight), a polysaccharide having β-1,4 linked D-xylose units, which can be substituted with other monosaccharide units. However, softwood contains hemicelluloses mainly in the form of glactoglucomannan (15%–20% dry weight), a polysaccharide having β,1–4 linked D-glucose, and D-galactose units (Bugg et al., 2011). Similarly, lignin is the most abundant and complex biopolymer in nature because of its low biodegradability, due to complex chemical bonding between its monomers resulted into recalcitrant compound of lignocellulosic materials (Wong, 2009). This is composed of phenylpropane units, which is synthesized by radical polymerization of guaiacyl units (G), syringyl units (S) and p-hydroxyphenyl units (H) from precursor coniferyl, sinapyl and p-coumaryl alcohol as shown Figure 1 (Horn et al., 2012). Lignin consists of high molecular weight aromatic polymer, containing numerous biologically stable ether or ester linkages. Thus cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix involving hemicellulose and lignin that hamper the way to cellulases and hemicellulases (Dimarogona et al., 2012). Due to its complexity, the degradation of lignocellulosic waste is a great challenge for sustainable development. The generation of lignocellulosic waste from various agro-based industries indicated the magnitude of problems including pulp and paper mill (effluent 150–200m3/ton and solid 160–450kg/ton), sugarcane molasses-based distilleries (effluent 15lit/1 lit alcohol production and 7.5 million tons/year), agricultural waste (200 billion tons/year), and food industry (1.3 billion ton/year) (Chandra et al., 2011; Gavrilescu, 2008; Kharayat, 2010; Kadam et al., 2013; Taha et al., 2016; Ravindran and Jaiswal, 2015). Due to their slow degradability and binding properties with other cationic molecules, they form complex compounds as environmental pollutants (Chandra et al., 2012; Dashtban et al., 2010). Therefore the lignocellulosic waste containing industrial waste is major source of environmental pollution (Sadh et al., 2018). The detail aquatic toxicity caused by pulp paper mill effluent has been also reported recently (Singh and Chandra, 2019). Besides, the adverse effects of lignocellulose containing wastewater have been reported for the reproductive system in fish i.e.masculinization, lower sex hormone, lower female vitellogenin, reduced gonad size, delayed maturity, circulation of sex hormones, fecundity, and modifications in secondary sexual characteristics to aquatic life (Chiang et al., 2015). In nature, efficient lignocellulosic waste degradation during process of wood decay becomes interesting due to characterization of potential fungi and bacteria that are reported by various researchers (Janusz et al., 2017). These lignocellulytic fungi and bacteria have own capabilities to produce several ligninolytic enzymes for the degradation of lignocellulosic waste (Sanchez, 2009Renugadevi et al., 2011). The degradation of cellulose and hemicellulose are complex in nature as it involves various enzymatic pathways and some of them also present in the form of insoluble crystalline fibers (Aarti et al., 2015). Degradation of crystalline cellulose is an enzymatic process including β–glucosidases, cellobiohydrolases, and β1-4-glucanases (Aarti et al., 2015). The degradation of cellulose and hemicellulose by various aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms has been reported with the production of carbon dioxide and glucose (Dimarogona et al., 2012). But the degradation of hemicelluloses requires different enzymes system (acetyl xylan, esterases, α-glucuronidases, β-D-xylosidases, and Endo-1,4-β-xylanases) (Vazquez et al., 2007). In general lignin-degrading enzymes have been divided into two major groups i.e. lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes and lignin modifying enzymes. Lignin degrading auxiliary enzymes are unable to degrade lignin on their own functions which need additional enzyme involvement for complete degradation (Janusz et al., 2017). Biological pretreatment strategies achieve selectivity by combining specific organisms or enzymatic systems with mild conditions that favor lignin degradation over cellulose destruction. The evidence points to three main pathways: oxidative, enzymatic, and mixed systems.

First, the main enzyme systems used are ligninolytic enzymes, especially laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase. These are described as playing a key role in the degradation of lignocellulosic waste and as central to ligninolytic activity [N2-R1]. The same review notes that lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes and lignin-modifying enzymes work sequentially, with some lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes needing additional enzymes for complete degradation [N2-F2]. This supports a mixed enzymatic strategy rather than a single-step hydrolytic process.

Second, the organisms most commonly associated with selective lignin degradation are white rot fungi and some bacteria. The review states that white rot fungi are highly selective for lignin and that ligninolytic bacteria and fungi have been reported to produce ligninolytic enzymes for lignocellulosic waste degradation [N2-F2]. It also notes that ligninolytic bacteria can transform heterogeneous lignin derivatives into value-added products [N2-R3]. This indicates that biological pretreatment is not limited to fungi alone, but can involve a broader microbial toolkit.

Third, the process is not purely hydrolytic. The evidence explicitly states that unlike hydrolytic processes, lignin degradation primarily involves oxidative reactions mediated by radicals [N1-F1]. This is a key distinction: oxidative pretreatment can preferentially target lignin’s radical-sensitive structure without necessarily breaking cellulose’s crystalline and hydrogen-bonded microfibrils. The same review also emphasizes that biological pretreatment is carried out under mild conditions, consuming less energy and avoiding the production of inhibitors that can interfere with downstream saccharification [N1-F1].

On conditions favoring lignin over cellulose destruction, the evidence is more about operational parameters than a single “selective” condition. The pretreatment literature shows that biological pretreatment can operate across a wide range of pH and temperature, with some strategies optimized around slightly acidic pH and moderate temperatures [N3-R1][N3-R5]. For example, one strain can decompose lignin at low temperature and over a broad pH range [N3-R3], while another optimal condition was culture temperature 35 °C and initial pH 7 [N3-R5]. These conditions suggest that mild, pH-tuned environments can favor lignin breakdown without excessive cellulose hydrolysis. The review also notes that biological pretreatment reduces lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, which helps preserve cellulose structure while still making it more accessible [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a selective biological pretreatment strategy based on oxidative and enzymatic pathways, mainly involving white rot fungi and ligninolytic bacteria, with mild conditions that favor lignin removal over cellulose destruction [N2-R1][N2-F2][N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5].

Selective lignin degradation in lignocellulosic biomass entails chemically and structurally targeted disruption of lignin while leaving cellulose largely intact. The evidence indicates that lignin is preferentially broken down because it is the most abundant and chemically complex biopolymer in nature, composed of phenylpropane units with complex chemical bonding that makes it recalcitrant [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that lignocellulosic waste degradation is difficult because of the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose and the unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin [N1-F1].

Chemically, the evidence points to preferential breakdown of lignin’s aromatic polymer structure. Lignin is described as a high-molecular-weight aromatic polymer containing numerous biologically stable ether or ester linkages [N2-F2]. The ligninolytic enzyme literature also identifies laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase as important in lignin depolymerization [N2-R1][N2-R5]. These enzymes are part of an oxidative lignin-degrading system rather than a simple hydrolytic one, which explains why lignin can be selectively degraded without cellulose necessarily being hydrolyzed [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The review further notes that lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes enable sequential action for complete degradation, implying that lignin is processed through a multi-step pathway rather than a single irreversible cleavage event [N2-F2].

Structurally, lignin removal exposes cellulose surfaces by disrupting the lignin-cellulose matrix. The evidence states that cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix involving hemicellulose and lignin, which hamper the access of cellulases and hemicellulases [N2-F2]. Pretreatment is described as a way to eliminate the compact and complex structure of biomass components, improve enzyme accessibility to cellulose, and promote dissociation of fibers [N1-F1]. The structural evidence also shows that pretreatment can reduce cellulose crystallinity and lignin content, which increases accessibility without fully dissolving cellulose [N1-F1].

Why cellulose remains intact during pretreatment is closely tied to its structural stability. Cellulose is a crystalline, hydrogen-bonded polymer with microfibrils formed by β-1,4-linked D-glucose units arranged in microfibrils stabilized by hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, such as decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This means that pretreatment can weaken lignin’s physical barrier and reduce cellulose crystallinity, making cellulose more accessible, while still preserving its overall molecular integrity [N1-F1][N1-R2].

In summary, selective lignin degradation entails chemically targeting lignin’s aromatic and cross-linked structure through oxidative and enzymatic systems, while structurally disrupting the lignin-cellulose matrix to expose cellulose surfaces. Cellulose remains intact because it is structurally more stable than lignin and is preserved by pretreatment conditions that reduce crystallinity and matrix obstruction rather than hydrolyzing the cellulose polymer itself [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R2].

Cellulose is preserved during biological pretreatment mainly because the process avoids excessive hydrolysis of the cellulose polymer and instead targets the lignin barrier surrounding it. The evidence shows that pretreatment can reduce lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, which helps improve accessibility without fully dissolving cellulose [N1-F1]. The review also notes that cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix with hemicellulose and lignin, and that pretreatment aims to eliminate the compact structure of biomass components so enzymes can access cellulose [N2-F2]. This means the preservation mechanism is structural and matrix-related, not because cellulose is inherently inert.

Mechanisms preventing cellulose hydrolysis include mild pretreatment conditions and the preservation of crystalline and hydrogen-bonded cellulose microfibrils. The evidence states that biological pretreatment is carried out under mild conditions and consumes less energy than traditional chemical pretreatment [N1-F1]. It also reports that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, including decreased crystallinity, which suggests that the pretreatment softens the structure rather than irreversibly hydrolyzing it [N1-R2]. The same review emphasizes that biological pretreatment does not produce inhibitors during treatment and is conducive to subsequent hydrolysis, indicating that the process avoids by-products that could otherwise interfere with cellulose hydrolysis [N1-F1].

The impact on enzymatic saccharification efficiency is clear. The review explicitly states that pretreatment is an effective approach to overcome the bottlenecks of lignocellulosic biomass by accelerating dissociation of fibers and promoting biomass conversion [N1-F1]. It also notes that pretreatment can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by reducing the lignin barrier and increasing accessibility to cellulose [N1-F1]. Additional evidence from a separate source reinforces that access to cellulose limits enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency, and pretreatments that reduce hemicellulose and lignin barriers can decrease cellulose crystallinity and enhance surface area and accessibility [N5-R1]. This means selective pretreatment improves saccharification efficiency by removing the physical and chemical obstruction around cellulose without destroying it.

Practically, this preservation has major implications for biofuel and bioproduct production. The review argues that biological pretreatment stands out because it is eco-friendly, consumes less energy, and avoids producing inhibitors [N1-F1]. The same source highlights that lignocellulose is an abundant renewable biomass resource with large-scale utilization potential, and that pretreatment improves the accessibility of polysaccharides into monosaccharides and promotes downstream hydrolysis and fermentation [N1-F1]. The evidence also shows that pretreatment can increase reducing sugar yields and improve enzymatic hydrolysis ability, supporting the idea that preserved cellulose translates into higher biomass conversion [N4-F3]. Taken together, preserving cellulose during pretreatment makes subsequent enzymatic saccharification more efficient and more economically viable for biofuel and bioproduct production [N1-F1][N5-R1][N4-F3].

Lignin-cellulose chemistry both limits and enables selective degradation, depending on the nature of the bond and the pretreatment approach. The evidence indicates that cellulose and lignin are not simply separate components; they are physically and chemically linked in the cell wall. The review states that cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix involving hemicellulose and lignin, and that the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose hinders enzymatic interactions [N2-F2]. Another source adds that the unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin inhibits enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-R5]. These statements show that direct physical and chemical bonding between lignin and cellulose is a major limitation because it blocks access to cellulose and interferes with hydrolysis [N2-F2][N5-R5].

Pretreatment disrupts lignin-cellulose bonding without breaking cellulose primarily through removal of the lignin barrier and reduction of lignin content. The review notes that pretreatment can reduce lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, and that it promotes dissociation of fibers and improves enzyme accessibility to cellulose [N1-F1]. It also states that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, including decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This suggests that pretreatment weakens the lignin-cellulose matrix and reduces lignin load, thereby exposing cellulose surfaces, but does not necessarily hydrolyze the cellulose polymer itself [N1-F1][N1-R2].

The role of pretreatment severity in lignin vs cellulose fate is important. The evidence shows that pretreatment severity is linked to biomass matrix opening and that pretreatment strategies span a wide range of reaction conditions, including pH and temperature [N3-R4]. At the same time, biological pretreatment is described as being carried out under mild conditions, consuming less energy, and avoiding inhibitor production [N1-F1]. This implies that lower severity can favor lignin removal while preserving cellulose, whereas higher severity may increase lignin degradation but also risk hydrolyzing cellulose. The review also notes that pretreatment can decrease lignin contents and cellulose crystallinity, but that the goal is to improve accessibility without excessively altering the cellulose structure [N1-F1]. Thus, pretreatment severity acts as a control knob: moderate conditions favor lignin removal and matrix disruption, while preserving cellulose integrity; extreme conditions risk over-degradation of both components.

In addition to physical disruption, lignin-cellulose chemistry can enable selectivity through specific binding interactions. The evidence on cellulose-lignin interactions indicates that lignin can selectively bind cellulose in a way that depends on lignin composition and cellulose face chemistry [N6-R3]. Molecular simulations are also cited as useful for examining cellulose binding face and lignin chemistry to build a quantitative lignin-cellulose interaction map [N6-R2]. These findings support the idea that lignin and cellulose do not form a uniform barrier; instead, their chemistry is heterogeneous and can be selectively altered by pretreatment [N6-R2][N6-R3]. This heterogeneity helps explain why pretreatment can remove lignin without necessarily dissolving cellulose [N6-R2].

Overall, lignin-cellulose chemistry limits selective degradation by physically and chemically linking the two components and by creating unproductive enzyme binding [N2-F2][N5-R5]. At the same time, pretreatment can disrupt this bonding through matrix opening and lignin removal, while preserving cellulose by acting on the lignin barrier rather than the cellulose polymer itself [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Pretreatment severity determines the balance between lignin removal and cellulose preservation, with mild conditions generally favored for selectivity [N1-F1][N3-R4].

Biological pretreatment selectively degrades lignin while preserving cellulose in lignocellulosic biomass by targeting the complex, barrier-forming lignin matrix rather than the crystalline cellulose itself. This selectivity arises from a combination of chemical, structural, and operational factors, and the evidence from the branch reports supports a unified mechanism in which lignin is preferentially broken down, cellulose is protected, and downstream processing becomes more efficient.

## 1) Chemically, lignin is preferentially targeted because it is the most recalcitrant component
The branch evidence shows that lignin is the most abundant and chemically complex biopolymer in lignocellulosic biomass, composed of phenylpropane units with complex chemical bonding that makes it highly recalcitrant [N2-F2]. This recalcitrance is what makes lignin a major barrier to enzymatic hydrolysis, because the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose hinders enzymatic interactions [N2-F2]. At the same time, lignin is not simply an inert polymer; it is a high-molecular-weight aromatic polymer containing numerous biologically stable ether or ester linkages, which are chemically labile to oxidative and enzymatic attack [N2-F2].

Biological pretreatment exploits this chemical complexity through ligninolytic enzymes, especially laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase, which are central to lignin degradation and detoxification of lignocellulosic waste [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also notes that lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes work sequentially, requiring additional enzymes for complete degradation [N2-F2]. This implies that lignin is processed through a multi-step pathway rather than a single irreversible cleavage event, which helps explain why biological pretreatment can preferentially target lignin without necessarily destroying cellulose.

## 2) Structurally, pretreatment disrupts the lignin-cellulose matrix and exposes cellulose surfaces
The structural explanation is that cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix involving hemicellulose and lignin, which physically prevents enzymes from accessing cellulose [N2-F2]. Pretreatment is therefore described as a way to eliminate the compact and complex structure of biomass components, improve enzyme accessibility to cellulose, and promote dissociation of fibers [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that pretreatment can reduce lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, which helps improve accessibility without fully dissolving cellulose [N1-F1].

A direct structural example from the branch reports is the p-toluenesulfonic acid-assisted hydrothermal pretreatment of poplar detritus, which increased cellulose accessibility, decreased lignin surface area, and weakened hydrophobicity, showing that pretreatment can remove lignin from the surface and expose cellulose [N4-F3]. Another line of evidence points to microstructural changes in cellulose, such as decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This means that the pretreatment softens the lignin-cellulose barrier rather than irreversibly hydrolyzing cellulose itself.

## 3) Why cellulose remains intact during pretreatment
Cellulose remains intact because it is structurally more stable than lignin and because pretreatment conditions are designed to preserve its crystalline and hydrogen-bonded microfibril structure. The evidence states that cellulose is a crystalline polymer formed by β-1,4-linked D-glucose units arranged in microfibrils stabilized by hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions [N2-F2]. Biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, including decreased crystallinity, but the same evidence suggests that this weakening is selective and does not necessarily destroy the cellulose polymer [N1-R2].

The preservation mechanism is therefore matrix-related: pretreatment targets the lignin barrier surrounding cellulose rather than the cellulose polymer itself. The review explicitly states that biological pretreatment is carried out under mild conditions, consumes less energy, and avoids producing inhibitors that could interfere with downstream saccharification [N1-F1]. This mildness is crucial because it minimizes the risk of cellulose hydrolysis while still improving accessibility. The same source also notes that the unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin inhibits enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-R5], reinforcing that cellulose is protected not because it is chemically inert, but because the pretreatment process avoids excessive hydrolysis and preserves the structural integrity of the cellulose microfibrils.

## 4) The biological pretreatment strategies that achieve selectivity
The branch reports identify several selective biological pretreatment strategies. The main enzyme systems used are ligninolytic enzymes, especially laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase, which are described as central to lignin degradation and detoxification [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also highlights that ligninolytic bacteria and fungi have been reported to produce ligninolytic enzymes for lignocellulosic waste degradation [N2-F2]. White rot fungi are especially noted as highly selective for lignin and are frequently associated with lignin degradation [N2-F2]. In addition, ligninolytic bacteria can transform heterogeneous lignin derivatives into value-added products, indicating that biological pretreatment is not limited to fungi alone [N2-R3].

The process is not purely hydrolytic. The evidence explicitly states that unlike hydrolytic processes, lignin degradation primarily involves oxidative reactions mediated by radicals [N1-F1]. This is an important distinction: oxidative pretreatment can selectively target lignin’s radical-sensitive structure without necessarily breaking cellulose. The same review also notes that biological pretreatment is carried out under mild conditions and does not produce inhibitors during treatment [N1-F1].

Conditions that favor lignin over cellulose destruction include mild pH and temperature. The evidence shows that biological pretreatment can operate across a wide range of pH and temperature, with some strategies optimized around slightly acidic pH and moderate temperatures [N3-R1][N3-R5]. For example, one strain can decompose lignin at low temperature and over a broad pH range [N3-R3], while another optimal condition was culture temperature 35 °C and initial pH 7 [N3-R5]. These conditions suggest that mild, pH-tuned environments can favor lignin breakdown without excessive cellulose hydrolysis. The review also notes that biological pretreatment reduces lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, which helps preserve cellulose structure while still making it more accessible [N1-F1].

## 5) Why cellulose preservation matters for downstream processing
Preserving cellulose is important because it improves enzymatic saccharification efficiency and makes downstream processing more viable. The review states that pretreatment is an effective approach to overcome the bottlenecks of lignocellulosic biomass by accelerating dissociation of fibers and promoting biomass conversion [N1-F1]. It also notes that pretreatment can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by reducing the lignin barrier and increasing accessibility to cellulose [N1-F1]. Additional evidence reinforces that access to cellulose limits enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency, and pretreatments that reduce hemicellulose and lignin barriers can decrease cellulose crystallinity and enhance surface area and accessibility [N5-R1].

Practically, this means that preserved cellulose translates into higher biomass conversion and better economic outcomes for biofuel and bioproduct production. The review argues that biological pretreatment stands out because it is eco-friendly, consumes less energy, and avoids producing inhibitors [N1-F1]. It also highlights that lignocellulose is an abundant renewable biomass resource with large-scale utilization potential, and that pretreatment improves the accessibility of polysaccharides into monosaccharides and promotes downstream hydrolysis and fermentation [N1-F1]. The evidence from the hydrothermal pretreatment study also shows that pretreatment can increase reducing sugar yields and improve enzymatic hydrolysis ability, supporting the idea that preserved cellulose enables higher productivity [N4-F3].

## 6) How lignin-cellulose chemistry limits and enables selective degradation
Lignin-cellulose chemistry both limits and enables selective degradation. On the one hand, the evidence indicates that cellulose and lignin are physically and chemically linked in the cell wall, and that the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose hinders enzymatic interactions [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin inhibits enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-R5]. These statements show that direct physical and chemical bonding between lignin and cellulose is a major limitation because it blocks access to cellulose and interferes with hydrolysis [N2-F2][N5-R5].

On the other hand, pretreatment can disrupt lignin-cellulose bonding without breaking cellulose. The review notes that pretreatment can reduce lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, and that it promotes dissociation of fibers and improves enzyme accessibility to cellulose [N1-F1]. It also states that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, including decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This suggests that pretreatment weakens the lignin-cellulose matrix and reduces lignin load, thereby exposing cellulose surfaces, but does not necessarily hydrolyze the cellulose polymer itself [N1-F1][N1-R2].

The role of pretreatment severity in lignin vs cellulose fate is therefore central. The evidence shows that pretreatment severity is linked to biomass matrix opening and that pretreatment strategies span a wide range of reaction conditions, including pH and temperature [N3-R4]. At the same time, biological pretreatment is described as being carried out under mild conditions, consuming less energy, and avoiding inhibitor production [N1-F1]. This implies that lower severity can favor lignin removal while preserving cellulose, whereas higher severity may increase lignin degradation but also risk hydrolyzing cellulose. The review also notes that pretreatment can decrease lignin contents and cellulose crystallinity, but that the goal is to improve accessibility without excessively altering the cellulose structure [N1-F1]. Thus, pretreatment severity acts as a control knob: moderate conditions favor lignin removal and matrix disruption, while preserving cellulose integrity; extreme conditions risk over-degradation of both components.

## 7) A more nuanced view: lignin-cellulose chemistry enables selectivity through heterogeneous binding
The evidence on cellulose-lignin interactions adds another layer to this explanation. It indicates that lignin can selectively bind cellulose in a way that depends on lignin composition and cellulose face chemistry [N6-R3]. Molecular simulations are also cited as useful for examining cellulose binding face and lignin chemistry to build a quantitative lignin-cellulose interaction map [N6-R2]. These findings support the idea that lignin and cellulose do not form a uniform barrier; instead, their chemistry is heterogeneous and can be selectively altered by pretreatment [N6-R2][N6-R3]. This heterogeneity helps explain why pretreatment can remove lignin without necessarily dissolving cellulose [N6-R2].

## Conclusion
Biological pretreatment selectively degrades lignin while preserving cellulose in lignocellulosic biomass through a combination of oxidative and enzymatic pathways, mild operating conditions, and structural matrix disruption. Lignin is preferentially targeted because it is chemically complex and recalcitrant, and because ligninolytic enzymes such as laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase are central to its degradation [N2-R1][N2-R5][N1-F1]. Pretreatment disrupts the lignin-cellulose matrix, reduces lignin content and lignin surface area, and improves cellulose accessibility without necessarily destroying the cellulose microfibril structure [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F3][N1-R2]. Cellulose remains intact because the process avoids excessive hydrolysis, preserves crystalline and hydrogen-bonded microfibrils, and is carried out under mild conditions that minimize inhibitor production [N1-F1][N5-R5]. The practical implication is that preserved cellulose leads to improved enzymatic saccharification efficiency and more economically viable biofuel and bioproduct production [N1-F1][N5-R1][N4-F3].

In short, biological pretreatment achieves selectivity not by directly hydrolyzing cellulose, but by removing the lignin barrier around it while preserving the structural integrity of cellulose itself [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F3].

Biological pretreatment strategies achieve selectivity by combining specific organisms or enzymatic systems with mild conditions that favor lignin degradation over cellulose destruction. The evidence points to three main pathways: oxidative, enzymatic, and mixed systems.

First, the main enzyme systems used are ligninolytic enzymes, especially laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase. These are described as playing a key role in the degradation of lignocellulosic waste and as central to ligninolytic activity [N2-R1]. The same review notes that lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes and lignin-modifying enzymes work sequentially, with some lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes needing additional enzymes for complete degradation [N2-F2]. This supports a mixed enzymatic strategy rather than a single-step hydrolytic process.

Second, the organisms most commonly associated with selective lignin degradation are white rot fungi and some bacteria. The review states that white rot fungi are highly selective for lignin and that ligninolytic bacteria and fungi have been reported to produce ligninolytic enzymes for lignocellulosic waste degradation [N2-F2]. It also notes that ligninolytic bacteria can transform heterogeneous lignin derivatives into value-added products [N2-R3]. This indicates that biological pretreatment is not limited to fungi alone, but can involve a broader microbial toolkit.

Third, the process is not purely hydrolytic. The evidence explicitly states that unlike hydrolytic processes, lignin degradation primarily involves oxidative reactions mediated by radicals [N1-F1]. This is a key distinction: oxidative pretreatment can preferentially target lignin’s radical-sensitive structure without necessarily breaking cellulose’s crystalline and hydrogen-bonded microfibrils. The same review also emphasizes that biological pretreatment is carried out under mild conditions, consuming less energy and avoiding the production of inhibitors that can interfere with downstream saccharification [N1-F1].

On conditions favoring lignin over cellulose destruction, the evidence is more about operational parameters than a single “selective” condition. The pretreatment literature shows that biological pretreatment can operate across a wide range of pH and temperature, with some strategies optimized around slightly acidic pH and moderate temperatures [N3-R1][N3-R5]. For example, one strain can decompose lignin at low temperature and over a broad pH range [N3-R3], while another optimal condition was culture temperature 35 °C and initial pH 7 [N3-R5]. These conditions suggest that mild, pH-tuned environments can favor lignin breakdown without excessive cellulose hydrolysis. The review also notes that biological pretreatment reduces lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, which helps preserve cellulose structure while still making it more accessible [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a selective biological pretreatment strategy based on oxidative and enzymatic pathways, mainly involving white rot fungi and ligninolytic bacteria, with mild conditions that favor lignin removal over cellulose destruction [N2-R1][N2-F2][N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5].

Selective lignin degradation in lignocellulosic biomass entails chemically and structurally targeted disruption of lignin while leaving cellulose largely intact. The evidence indicates that lignin is preferentially broken down because it is the most abundant and chemically complex biopolymer in nature, composed of phenylpropane units with complex chemical bonding that makes it recalcitrant [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that lignocellulosic waste degradation is difficult because of the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose and the unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin [N1-F1].

Chemically, the evidence points to preferential breakdown of lignin’s aromatic polymer structure. Lignin is described as a high-molecular-weight aromatic polymer containing numerous biologically stable ether or ester linkages [N2-F2]. The ligninolytic enzyme literature also identifies laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase as important in lignin depolymerization [N2-R1][N2-R5]. These enzymes are part of an oxidative lignin-degrading system rather than a simple hydrolytic one, which explains why lignin can be selectively degraded without cellulose necessarily being hydrolyzed [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The review further notes that lignin-degrading auxiliary enzymes enable sequential action for complete degradation, implying that lignin is processed through a multi-step pathway rather than a single irreversible cleavage event [N2-F2].

Structurally, lignin removal exposes cellulose surfaces by disrupting the lignin-cellulose matrix. The evidence states that cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix involving hemicellulose and lignin, which hamper the access of cellulases and hemicellulases [N2-F2]. Pretreatment is described as a way to eliminate the compact and complex structure of biomass components, improve enzyme accessibility to cellulose, and promote dissociation of fibers [N1-F1]. The structural evidence also shows that pretreatment can reduce cellulose crystallinity and lignin content, which increases accessibility without fully dissolving cellulose [N1-F1].

Why cellulose remains intact during pretreatment is closely tied to its structural stability. Cellulose is a crystalline, hydrogen-bonded polymer with microfibrils formed by β-1,4-linked D-glucose units arranged in microfibrils stabilized by hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, such as decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This means that pretreatment can weaken lignin’s physical barrier and reduce cellulose crystallinity, making cellulose more accessible, while still preserving its overall molecular integrity [N1-F1][N1-R2].

In summary, selective lignin degradation entails chemically targeting lignin’s aromatic and cross-linked structure through oxidative and enzymatic systems, while structurally disrupting the lignin-cellulose matrix to expose cellulose surfaces. Cellulose remains intact because it is structurally more stable than lignin and is preserved by pretreatment conditions that reduce crystallinity and matrix obstruction rather than hydrolyzing the cellulose polymer itself [N2-F2][N1-F1][N1-R2].

The evidence indicates that cellulose and lignin are not simply separate components; they are physically and chemically linked in the cell wall. The review states that cellulose microfibrils are embedded in a complex matrix involving hemicellulose and lignin, and that the complex cross-linked structure of lignocellulose hinders enzymatic interactions [N2-F2]. Another source adds that the unproductive binding between enzymes and lignin inhibits enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-R5]. These statements show that direct physical and chemical bonding between lignin and cellulose is a major limitation because it blocks access to cellulose and interferes with hydrolysis [N2-F2][N5-R5].

Pretreatment disrupts lignin-cellulose bonding without breaking cellulose primarily through removal of the lignin barrier and reduction of lignin content. The review notes that pretreatment can reduce lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, and that it promotes dissociation of fibers and improves enzyme accessibility to cellulose [N1-F1]. It also states that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, including decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This suggests that pretreatment weakens the lignin-cellulose matrix and reduces lignin load, thereby exposing cellulose surfaces, but does not necessarily hydrolyze the cellulose polymer itself [N1-F1][N1-R2].

The role of pretreatment severity in lignin vs cellulose fate is important. The evidence shows that pretreatment severity is linked to biomass matrix opening and that pretreatment strategies span a wide range of reaction conditions, including pH and temperature [N3-R4]. At the same time, biological pretreatment is described as being carried out under mild conditions, consuming less energy, and avoiding inhibitor production [N1-F1]. This implies that lower severity can favor lignin removal while preserving cellulose, whereas higher severity may increase lignin degradation but also risk hydrolyzing cellulose. The review also notes that pretreatment can decrease lignin contents and cellulose crystallinity, but that the goal is to improve accessibility without excessively altering the cellulose structure [N1-F1]. Thus, pretreatment severity acts as a control knob: moderate conditions favor lignin removal and matrix disruption, while preserving cellulose integrity; extreme conditions risk over-degradation of both components.

In addition to physical disruption, lignin-cellulose chemistry can enable selectivity through specific binding interactions. The evidence on cellulose-lignin interactions indicates that lignin can selectively bind cellulose in a way that depends on lignin composition and cellulose face chemistry [N6-R3]. Molecular simulations are also cited as useful for examining cellulose binding face and lignin chemistry to build a quantitative lignin-cellulose interaction map [N6-R2]. These findings support the idea that lignin and cellulose do not form a uniform barrier; instead, their chemistry is heterogeneous and can be selectively altered by pretreatment [N6-R2][N6-R3]. This heterogeneity helps explain why pretreatment can remove lignin without necessarily dissolving cellulose [N6-R2].

Overall, lignin-cellulose chemistry limits selective degradation by physically and chemically linking the two components and by creating unproductive enzyme binding [N2-F2][N5-R5]. At the same time, pretreatment can disrupt this bonding through matrix opening and lignin removal, while preserving cellulose by acting on the lignin barrier rather than the cellulose polymer itself [N1-F1][N1-R2]. These statements show that direct physical and chemical bonding between lignin and cellulose is a major limitation because it blocks access to cellulose and interferes with hydrolysis [N2-F2][N5-R5].

On the other hand, pretreatment can disrupt lignin-cellulose bonding without breaking cellulose. The review notes that pretreatment can reduce lignin content, cellulose crystallinity, and energy consumption, and that it promotes dissociation of fibers and improves enzyme accessibility to cellulose [N1-F1]. It also states that biological pretreatment can cause microstructural changes of cellulose, including decreased crystallinity, without necessarily breaking the microfibril structure [N1-R2]. This suggests that pretreatment weakens the lignin-cellulose matrix and reduces lignin load, thereby exposing cellulose surfaces, but does not necessarily hydrolyze the cellulose polymer itself [N1-F1][N1-R2].

The role of pretreatment severity in lignin vs cellulose fate is therefore central. The evidence shows that pretreatment severity is linked to biomass matrix opening and that pretreatment strategies span a wide range of reaction conditions, including pH and temperature [N3-R4]. At the same time, biological pretreatment is described as being carried out under mild conditions, consuming less energy, and avoiding inhibitor production [N1-F1]. This implies that lower severity can favor lignin removal while preserving cellulose, whereas higher severity may increase lignin degradation but also risk hydrolyzing cellulose. The review also notes that pretreatment can decrease lignin contents and cellulose crystallinity, but that the goal is to improve accessibility without excessively altering the cellulose structure [N1-F1]. Thus, pretreatment severity acts as a control knob: moderate conditions favor lignin removal and matrix disruption, while preserving cellulose integrity; extreme conditions risk over-degradation of both components.

## 7) A more nuanced view: lignin-cellulose chemistry enables selectivity through heterogeneous binding
The evidence on cellulose-lignin interactions adds another layer to this explanation. It indicates that lignin can selectively bind cellulose in a way that depends on lignin composition and cellulose face chemistry [N6-R3]. Molecular simulations are also cited as useful for examining cellulose binding face and lignin chemistry to build a quantitative lignin-cellulose interaction map [N6-R2]. These findings support the idea that lignin and cellulose do not form a uniform barrier; instead, their chemistry is heterogeneous and can be selectively altered by pretreatment [N6-R2][N6-R3]. This heterogeneity helps explain why pretreatment can remove lignin without necessarily dissolving cellulose [N6-R2].

## Conclusion
Biological pretreatment selectively degrades lignin while preserving cellulose in lignocellulosic biomass through a combination of oxidative and enzymatic pathways, mild operating conditions, and structural matrix disruption. Lignin is preferentially targeted because it is chemically complex and recalcitrant, and because ligninolytic enzymes such as laccase, lignin peroxidase, and manganese peroxidase are central to its degradation [N2-R1][N2-R5][N1-F1]. Pretreatment disrupts the lignin-cellulose matrix, reduces lignin content and lignin surface area, and improves cellulose accessibility without necessarily destroying the cellulose microfibril structure [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F3][N1-R2]. Cellulose remains intact because the process avoids excessive hydrolysis, preserves crystalline and hydrogen-bonded microfibrils, and is carried out under mild conditions that minimize inhibitor production [N1-F1][N5-R5]. The practical implication is that preserved cellulose leads to improved enzymatic saccharification efficiency and more economically viable biofuel and bioproduct production [N1-F1][N5-R1][N4-F3].

In short, biological pretreatment achieves selectivity not by directly hydrolyzing cellulose, but by removing the lignin barrier around it while preserving the structural integrity of cellulose itself [N2-F2][N1-F1][N4-F3].
